paragraphs.heading: What gets written down
paragraphs.text: A mineral is, broadly speaking, a solid substance that occurs naturally in pure form. Its chemical composition is fairly well defined, and it has a specific crystal structure. Composition and structure are the essentials of any mineral species. A description usually adds the mineral's common physical properties. Habit, hardness, lustre, colour, streak, cleavage, fracture, specific gravity, magnetism, fluorescence and radioactivity are all among them. A description can also record a mineral's taste or smell and how it reacts to acid.

paragraphs.heading: Structure shows on the outside
paragraphs.text: Every mineral needs a well-defined crystallographic structure, which more generally means its atoms are arranged in an ordered way. This requirement implies several macroscopic, or large-scale, physical properties, such as crystal form, hardness and cleavage. It also shuts out amorphous materials, meaning ones that are not crystalline. Obsidian, limonite and ozokerite are excluded on this ground. Opal and obsidian are natural solids that lack a definite crystalline structure, and such substances are more properly called mineraloids.

paragraphs.heading: Same compound, different mineral
paragraphs.text: Sometimes one chemical compound is found in nature with more than one crystal structure. Each of those structures then counts as a separate mineral species. Quartz and stishovite are an example. Both consist of the same compound, silicon dioxide, yet they are two different minerals.

paragraphs.heading: Composition with some give
paragraphs.text: A mineral must also have a fairly well defined chemical composition. Even so, some crystalline substances whose structure is fixed but whose composition varies may be treated as a single mineral species. Solid solutions such as mackinawite, (Fe, Ni)₉S₈, are a common class of examples. Mackinawite is mostly a ferrous sulfide in which nickel atoms have taken the place of a significant fraction of the iron atoms. The reverse also happens: a substance whose compositions form a continuous series may be divided, arbitrarily, into several minerals. In the olivine group, (Mg, Fe)₂SiO₄, the magnesium-rich end-member and the iron-rich one are counted as separate minerals, forsterite and fayalite.

paragraphs.heading: Solid, with one exception
paragraphs.text: A mineral must be a solid in its natural occurrence. Native mercury is a major exception to this rule. It crystallizes only below −39 °C, but the International Mineralogical Association (IMA) still classifies it as a mineral, since it was included before the current rules were set. Water and carbon dioxide are not considered minerals, though they are often found as inclusions inside other minerals. Water ice, however, is considered a mineral.

paragraphs.heading: How stable it has to be
paragraphs.text: Some authors require that a mineral be solid, and stable or metastable, at room temperature, 25 °C. The IMA asks for less: the substance only needs enough stability that its structure and composition can be well determined. Meridianiite is an example. It is a natural hydrate of magnesium sulfate that forms and stays stable only below 2 °C, and the IMA recognizes it as a mineral.
